fichas.title: Historical Review of Theatres
fichas.summary: Theatre design involves complex functional relationships shaped by a tradition extending across many societies. The page surveys ancient, medieval, and Renaissance theatre forms, including audience arrangements, stages, and scenery systems.

fichas.title: Ancient Greek and Roman Theatres
fichas.summary: Greek theatres were located near towns and embedded in the landscape. The Theatre of Dionysos is presented as the starting point of European theatre building. The Theatre of Marcellus was Rome’s first theatre built completely of stone, with seating rows and the stage’s back wall connected at the same height.

fichas.title: Medieval Stage Theatre and Swan Theatre
fichas.summary: Medieval theatre could use temporary stages and buildings. At the Swan Theatre, a curtain separated the front and back stages, while an upper stage served for balcony or siege scenes. The drawing also identifies changing rooms, backstage, orchestra, proscenium, and audience areas organized by social rank.

Historical Review

The design of theatres requires an understanding of complex
functional interactions, of which much is explained by the history
of theatres. This is an architectural challenge, which has been
interpreted by various societies for more than 2500 years. Each
theatre building today stands in a great tradition, even if it is
marked by efforts to escape from this. A few examples should
throw light on the historical development of this type of building -'>

fichas.title: Renaissance Theatres
fichas.summary: Early Italian Renaissance theatres were temporary wooden installations in existing halls. The page describes Vasari’s reusable wooden system, Teatro Olimpico as a permanent theatre reviving ancient traditions with semicircular rising audience seating and a stage house with façade, and Teatro Farnese as the first building with a movable scenery system in a deep stage space. The Teatro Farnese audience boxes were arranged in a horseshoe.
